newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Northern Afghan city tense under Taleban rule.
newsitem.headline: Northern Afghan city tense under Taleban rule.

text.p: Schools and a number of shops remained closed in this northern Afghan city, controlled by an uneasy alliance of the Islamic Taleban militia and ethnic Uzbek troops who recently changed sides.

Soldiers loyal to General Abdul Malik, who drove the Jumbish-i-Milli faction leader General Abdul Rashid Dostum out of the north last week, have little in common with the ethnic Pashtun Taleban fighters who swarmed into the town on Sunday.
"Trouble is not over yet," said one foreign resident, who asked not to be named. "People were smiling when Malik's troops arrived, but now they fear that Taleban will disarm them."
Shopkeepers hastily closed their shutters and passersby scattered briefly in a central area on Tuesday, apparently after an argument between Taleban and Malik's fighters.

The airport has not reopened for U.N. or Red Cross flights since Mazar-i-Sharif fell on Saturday, but Pakistan's ambassador flew in on Monday and military aircraft, including a plane that brought in 160 Taleban on Tuesday, have been using it. U.N. agencies have yet to resume their normal activities and most international staff were staying at home.

The Taleban, which along with its allies now control some 90 percent of Afghanistan, have wasted little time issuing edicts to enforce their idea of the Islamic Sharia law in a city that pursued a relatively liberal lifestyle when Dostum was in power.
Broadcasts from mosque loudspeakers have told women to stay at home. They may go out only if they wear an all-enveloping burqa robe and are accompanied by close male relatives.
Women employees must stay at home, for at least a week, although the Taleban said their salaries would be paid, and all men must grow beards. The Taleban also banned music.
Malik's troops were guarding the deserted campus of the city's Balkh University, where students of both sexes were attending classes until the end of last week.

When the university reopens, only men would be allowed to return, in line with Taleban policy that girls and women must wait until security improves and there is enough money to provide separate educational facilities for them.

Mohammad Hakeem, owner of one of the countless photo shops in Mazar-i-Sharif, said he had reopened on Tuesday, but did not know if the Taleban, who believe taking pictures of humans is un-Islamic, will allow him to stay in business.
"If not, I will look for another job," he said with a smile.

At the civil hospital, the health director for north Afghanistan, Faisal Mohammad Wardak, said health facilities would now have to be segregated, adding that more than a third of the 1,061 health workers in the north were women.
"The problem of women doctors will be solved very soon," he said. "We will set aside one hospital in Mazar-i-Sharif that will be only for women patients with women doctors and nurses."
Across the courtyard, two female burns victims lay on cots in a bare concrete room, one of them moaning as she was tended by relatives amid an awful stench.
"We have no medicine. There is a prescription in my pocket, but I have spent my money," said Rasul, the father of one of the burnt women, named Famila.
Her sister Sarah said Famila had been in hospital for 45 days after accidentally pouring kerosene, instead of cooking oil, on to a pot she was heating on a kerosene stove.
"I want to commit suicide," Sarah wept. "I hate this life."
